title: Airway Bacterium May Prime Lungs to Repel Pneumonia, Study Finds
title_zh: 研究发现：气道细菌或能帮肺部提前“备战”肺炎
lead: A bacterium commonly found in the mouth and airways may quietly train the lungs' immune defenses, according to new research. The findings could reshape how scientists think about preventing bacterial pneumonia.

paragraphs: New research from the University of Colorado Anschutz suggests that Prevotella melaninogenica, a bacterium routinely present in healthy airways, may sharpen the lungs' ability to fend off pneumonia. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study found that exposing mice to P. melaninogenica altered the behavior of pulmonary immune cells. When the animals were subsequently challenged with Streptococcus pneumoniae, a leading cause of bacterial pneumonia, their immune systems proved markedly more adept at recognizing, engulfing and clearing the pathogen.

That exposure to S. pneumoniae does not invariably precipitate severe illness has long puzzled researchers, who have increasingly suspected that the respiratory microbiome—the community of microorganisms inhabiting the airway—helps determine how effectively someone resists infection. Prevotella, one of the most prevalent bacterial groups in the healthy mouth and respiratory tract, has previously been linked to better outcomes in people with respiratory infections, yet the mechanism behind this protective association remained obscure.

To probe it, Sarah Clark, Ph.D., senior author and associate professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine, and her colleagues exposed mice to P. melaninogenica before challenging them with S. pneumoniae. Using single-cell RNA sequencing to scrutinize thousands of individual lung cells, the team observed that Prevotella exposure had effectively reprogrammed several types of immune cells. Neutrophils and macrophages in the exposed mice engulfed and killed S. pneumoniae more efficiently, and the animals harbored significantly lower amounts of pneumonia-causing bacteria in their lungs.

"Our lungs encounter bacteria from our mouths and upper airways all the time, and those exposures may actually be helping to educate the immune system," Clark said. "We found that exposure to P. melaninogenica changes the way immune cells respond, essentially putting them in a better position to fight a bacterial infection." She added that the immune cells were present in greater numbers and behaving differently—functionally reprogrammed to clear bacteria more effectively.

The study bolsters mounting evidence that bacteria native to the respiratory tract are not merely passive passengers but may actively shape immune responses to disease. Clinical studies have associated greater respiratory microbial diversity, and the presence of anaerobic bacteria such as Prevotella, with better outcomes in severe respiratory illness; the new findings offer a plausible biological explanation. Whether this natural interaction can be harnessed to prevent respiratory infections, Clark said, is the next question.
paragraphs_zh: 科罗拉多大学安舒茨分校的新研究提出，一种常驻健康气道的细菌——黑色素普雷沃菌（Prevotella melaninogenica）——或许能增强肺部抵御肺炎的能力。该研究发表于《美国国家科学院院刊》，发现让小鼠接触这种细菌后，其肺部免疫细胞的行为发生了变化。随后当这些小鼠遭遇肺炎链球菌（细菌性肺炎的主要致病菌）时，它们的免疫系统明显更擅长识别、吞噬并清除病原体。
接触肺炎链球菌并不总会导致重病，这一直令研究人员困惑。他们越来越怀疑，呼吸道微生物组——即栖息在气道中的微生物群落——在决定一个人抵抗感染的效果方面起着重要作用。普雷沃菌是健康口腔和呼吸道中最常见的细菌类群之一，此前已被发现与呼吸道感染者较好的预后相关，但这种保护性关联背后的机制始终不明。
为探究其中机理，资深作者、科罗拉多大学安舒茨医学院副教授萨拉·克拉克博士及其同事先让小鼠接触黑色素普雷沃菌，再让它们感染肺炎链球菌。研究团队利用单细胞RNA测序技术仔细分析数千个肺部单个细胞，观察到接触普雷沃菌实际上重新编程了多种免疫细胞。接触过该菌的小鼠体内，中性粒细胞和巨噬细胞吞噬、杀灭肺炎链球菌的效率更高，肺中致病菌的数量也显著更低。
克拉克说：“我们的肺时刻都在接触来自口腔和上呼吸道的细菌，这些接触可能实际上是在帮助‘教育’免疫系统。我们发现，接触黑色素普雷沃菌改变了免疫细胞的反应方式，本质上让它们处于更有利于对抗细菌感染的状态。”她补充说，这些免疫细胞数量更多，行为也不同——经过功能性重编程，能更有效地清除细菌。
这项研究进一步支持了越来越多的证据：呼吸道原生的细菌并非单纯的“搭便车者”，而可能主动塑造免疫系统对疾病的反应。临床研究已将呼吸道微生物多样性更高、以及普雷沃菌等厌氧菌的存在，与严重呼吸道疾病较好的预后联系起来；新发现为这些观察提供了合理的生物学解释。克拉克表示，能否利用这种微生物组与免疫系统之间的自然互动来预防呼吸道感染，是下一个问题。

A common bacterium found in the mouth and airways may help the lungs better defend themselves against pneumonia, according to new research from the University of Colorado Anschutz.
The study, published in
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
, found that exposure to Prevotella melaninogenica (P. melaninogenica), a type of bacterium commonly found in healthy airways, changed the behavior of immune cells in the lungs of mice. When the mice were later exposed to Streptococcus pneumoniae, a leading cause of bacterial pneumonia, their immune systems were better able to recognize, engulf and clear the bacteria.
The findings offer new insight into why some people are more resilient to respiratory infections than others and could eventually point toward new ways of strengthening the lungs' natural defenses against pneumonia.
"Our lungs encounter bacteria from our mouths and upper airways all the time, and those exposures may actually be helping to educate the immune system," said Sarah Clark, Ph.D., senior author and associate professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine. "We found that exposure to P. melaninogenica changes the way immune cells respond, essentially putting them in a better position to fight a bacterial infection."
Preparing the immune system
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major cause of pneumonia, but exposure to the bacterium does not always lead to serious illness. Researchers have increasingly suspected that the community of microorganisms living throughout the airway, known as the respiratory microbiome, may play an important role in determining how well someone fights an infection.
Prevotella is one of the most common groups of bacteria found in the healthy mouth and respiratory tract. Previous research has found that higher levels of Prevotella are associated with better outcomes in people with respiratory infections.
But scientists did not know exactly how the bacterium might help protect against pneumonia.
To investigate, Clark and her colleagues exposed mice to P. melaninogenica and then challenged them with S. pneumoniae. The researchers used
single-cell RNA sequencing
to examine thousands of individual cells in the lungs and determine how their activity changed.
The results showed that Prevotella exposure essentially reprogrammed several types of immune cells involved in fighting infection.
In mice exposed to Prevotella, immune cells called neutrophils and macrophages were better at engulfing and killing S. pneumoniae. The mice also had significantly lower amounts of the pneumonia-causing bacteria in their lungs.
"The immune cells were present in greater numbers and behaving differently," Clark said. "They had been functionally reprogrammed to do a better job of clearing bacteria."
The lung microbiome may be part of the body's first line of defense
The study adds to growing evidence that bacteria normally found in the respiratory tract are not simply passive passengers. Instead, they may actively influence how the immune system responds to disease.
The researchers note that clinical studies have linked greater respiratory microbial diversity and the presence of anaerobic bacteria such as Prevotella with better outcomes in people with severe respiratory illness.
The new findings provide a possible biological explanation for those observations.
"We're interested in understanding whether we can harness this natural interaction between the microbiome and the immune system," Clark said. "If we can figure out how these bacteria educate immune cells to respond more effectively, it could open up entirely new approaches to preventing respiratory infections."
